title: Linear Search
summary: Learn linear search by checking one item at a time. Trace a small list, handle missing values, and compare working code in six languages.
introduction: Imagine looking for a red pencil in your bag. You check one pencil, then the next, until you find it. Linear search does this with a list. We will search a few numbers and return the position of the first match.
learningObjectives: Find the first matching position in a list
Explain why a missing value may need every item checked

blocks.text: An algorithm is a clear set of steps. Linear search checks items from left to right. It works even when the numbers are in a mixed order.
An index is an item's position. These languages count positions from 0. We return the matching index, or -1 when no item matches. The value -1 is a signal here; it is not a position to read.

items: Start with [9, 4, 7, 4] and look for 7. Position 0 holds 9, so keep looking.
Position 1 holds 4. It is not 7, so move one step.
Position 2 holds 7. Return 2 and stop. The last item does not need a check.
Now look for 6. Check all four items. None match, so return -1.

blocks.text: The same program in six languages

Choose the language you are learning. Each tab solves the same problem and prints the same result. JavaScript can run in this page. The other tabs need separate local tools: a C11 compiler, a C++17 compiler, Python 3, .NET 8 or later for C#, or Java 17. Use Program.cs for C# and Main.java for Java.
The first line is 2 because 7 is the third item and positions start at 0. The second line is -1 because the list does not contain 6.
An empty list has no item to check, so the function returns -1. If a value appears twice, this version returns the first match. Searching for 4 returns 1.
Use one kind of value, such as small whole numbers. In C, pass the true item count as n; an array parameter does not carry its length.
How much work and extra room?
Let n mean the number of items. In the worst case, we check n items. We call this O(n) time: doubling the list can double the checks. A match at the first item needs one check, or O(1) best time.
The function keeps only an index and the target. It does not copy the list. Its extra space is O(1), which means a fixed amount of room as the list grows.

blocks.title: Try one small change
blocks.text: Change the first target from 7 to 4. Predict 1 before running. Then try a value outside the list and check that you get -1.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Do not return -1 after the first non-match. A later item may still match. Put that return after the loop. Also check for -1 before using a returned position.
